body:
Biological information and food production

Biological research investigates how living organisms function, reproduce and pass characteristics to the next generation. Applied agricultural research uses scientific knowledge to improve crops and food production.

The achievements of H. Gobind Khorana, Venkatraman Ramakrishnan and M. S. Swaminathan illustrate these related but distinct fields.

H. Gobind Khorana: The genetic code

Har Gobind Khorana (1922-2011) was an Indian-born biochemist. He made major contributions to understanding the genetic code, which connects genetic information with the sequence of amino acids used to make proteins.

DNA contains hereditary information. During protein production, that information is conveyed through RNA. Groups of 3 nucleotides in messenger RNA, called codons, specify amino acids or signal the end of protein synthesis.

Khorana shared the 1968 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with Robert W. Holley and Marshall W. Nirenberg for the interpretation of the genetic code and its function in protein synthesis.

Venkatraman Ramakrishnan: The ribosome

Venkatraman Ramakrishnan is a structural biologist associated with the study of ribosomes. Ribosomes are cellular structures that use information carried by messenger RNA to assemble amino acids into proteins.

His research helped reveal the structure and functioning of the ribosome. He shared the 2009 Nobel Prize in Chemistry with Thomas A. Steitz and Ada E. Yonath.

Ramakrishnan has an important Gujarat connection. He grew up in Vadodara and earned a bachelor's degree in physics from the Maharaja Sayajirao University of Baroda. However, he was born in Chidambaram, Tamil Nadu, not in Gujarat.

Khorana: genetic code and its role in protein synthesis, Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, 1968. Ramakrishnan: structure and function of ribosomes, Nobel Prize in Chemistry, 2009.

M. S. Swaminathan: Agricultural science

Mankombu Sambasivan Swaminathan (1925-2023) was an Indian agricultural scientist widely associated with the Green Revolution in India. During the 1960s, agricultural science, including the development and adoption of high-yielding crop varieties, helped raise food-grain production.

Swaminathan played an important role in promoting improvements in crop production, particularly through agricultural research and the use of improved wheat varieties. Higher-yielding seeds were used alongside irrigation, fertilisers and other farming inputs. The success of the Green Revolution therefore cannot be attributed to seeds alone.

Swaminathan was awarded the Bharat Ratna in 2024, posthumously.

Matching the contributions

ScientistFieldImportant recognition
H. Gobind KhoranaBiochemistry and genetic codeNobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, 1968
Venkatraman RamakrishnanStructural biology and ribosomesNobel Prize in Chemistry, 2009
M. S. SwaminathanAgricultural scienceBharat Ratna, 2024

Prelims focus

  • H. Gobind Khorana: genetic code; 1968 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
  • Venkatraman Ramakrishnan: ribosome; 2009 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
  • Ramakrishnan studied in Vadodara but was born in Tamil Nadu.
  • M. S. Swaminathan: Green Revolution in India.
  • Swaminathan received the Bharat Ratna in 2024.
  • Trap: A genetic code is not the same thing as a ribosome.

[Sources: Nobel Prize, 'The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 1968,' prize citation for Holley, Khorana and Nirenberg; Nobel Prize, 'The Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2009,' press release dated 7 October 2009; Nobel Prize, 'Venkatraman Ramakrishnan: Biographical,' sections 'Childhood' and 'Choosing Basic Science'; Maharaja Sayajirao University of Baroda, Distinguished Alumni, 'Shri Venkatraman,' education section; Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare, release on the Bharat Ratna for M. S. Swaminathan, 13 February 2024. Online sources consulted 2 November 2026.]

title: Indian Achievements in Genetics, Ribosome Research and Agriculture

body:
Basic research and atomic energy

Homi Jehangir Bhabha (1909-1966) was an Indian physicist and institution-builder. He made important contributions to scientific research and played a leading role in establishing India's atomic energy programme. He is commonly described as the father of India's nuclear programme.

Atomic energy is associated with processes involving the nuclei of atoms. Basic scientific research investigates fundamental questions about nature, whereas an applied research programme uses scientific knowledge to develop technologies and practical capabilities. Bhabha recognised the need for both strong basic-science institutions and a coordinated atomic energy programme.

Tata Institute of Fundamental Research

Bhabha established the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research (TIFR) with support from the Sir Dorabji Tata Trust. It began functioning on 1 June 1945 at the Indian Institute of Science in Bangalore, now Bengaluru, and moved to Bombay, now Mumbai, later that year.

TIFR was established to support advanced research in fundamental sciences. Its work has included physics, mathematics and other scientific disciplines. It is not limited to research on nuclear power.

Atomic Energy Commission and Department of Atomic Energy

The Atomic Energy Commission (AEC) was established in 1948, with Bhabha as its first chairman. The Commission was associated with the development and coordination of India's atomic energy activities.

The Department of Atomic Energy (DAE) was established in 1954. It provided an administrative framework for the country's atomic energy programme.

The distinction is important: the AEC is a commission, while the DAE is a government department. Neither name refers to the same institution as the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre.

From AEET to BARC

Bhabha established the Atomic Energy Establishment, Trombay (AEET) in 1954. It became a major centre for research and development associated with atomic energy.

After Bhabha's death in 1966, AEET was renamed the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) in 1967, in his memory. BARC is located at Trombay, Mumbai, Maharashtra.

TIFR and BARC are different institutions. TIFR was established in 1945 for fundamental research. AEET was established in 1954 and renamed BARC in 1967. The renaming did not mark the original establishment of the research centre.

Why Bhabha's contribution matters

Bhabha's role was not confined to a single experiment or discovery. He helped create scientific institutions, research programmes and trained scientific communities. These provided a foundation for India's long-term capabilities in atomic science and related areas.

Prelims focus

  • Homi J. Bhabha: father of India's nuclear programme.
  • TIFR: established on 1 June 1945.
  • Atomic Energy Commission: established in 1948.
  • Department of Atomic Energy: established in 1954.
  • AEET: established in 1954; renamed BARC in 1967.
  • Trap: BARC is in Mumbai, not Ahmedabad or Gandhinagar.

[Sources: Tata Institute of Fundamental Research, 'History and Vision,' sections on founding and the 1945 relocation; Bhabha Atomic Research Centre, 'Former Directors,' biographical entry for Homi J. Bhabha; Bhabha Atomic Research Centre, historical account of the 1948 Atomic Energy Commission and establishment of DAE and AEET in 1954; BARC Newsletter, January 2006, 'BARC History,' p. 12, on the 1967 renaming. Online sources consulted 2 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Timeline of Bhabha’s institutions, highlighting AEET’s establishment in 1954 and its renaming as BARC in 1967, after his death in 1966.
pictures.caption: Major institutional milestones associated with Homi J. Bhabha.

title: Homi J. Bhabha and the Foundations of India's Atomic Energy Programme

body:
A scientist from Ahmedabad

Vikram Ambalal Sarabhai (1919-1971) was born on 12 August 1919 in Ahmedabad, Gujarat. He was a physicist and scientific institution-builder and is widely known as the father of the Indian space programme.

Sarabhai studied cosmic rays, which are energetic particles arriving from space. Research on cosmic rays helps scientists understand high-energy natural phenomena and their interactions with the Earth's atmosphere.

He worked with the Nobel Prize-winning physicist C. V. Raman at the Indian Institute of Science. This provides an important connection between Raman's contribution to Indian physics and Sarabhai's later leadership in space research.

Establishment of the Physical Research Laboratory

Sarabhai founded the Physical Research Laboratory (PRL) in 1947. The laboratory was formally established on 11 November 1947 at M. G. Science College in Ahmedabad.

Its early research focused on cosmic rays and the upper atmosphere. Over time, PRL expanded into fields including astronomy, planetary science and other areas of fundamental physics.

PRL is an institution devoted to scientific research. Its primary identity should not be confused with a centre that develops satellite communication instruments or other applied space technologies.

Development of India's space programme

Sarabhai believed space science and technology could support national development, including education, communication and the study of natural resources.

In 1962, the Indian National Committee for Space Research (INCOSPAR) was formed, and Sarabhai led the country's early organised space research activities. The Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) was established on 15 August 1969, building on this earlier programme.

In 1966, an experimental satellite communication earth-station initiative was developed in Ahmedabad under Sarabhai's leadership. Several Ahmedabad-based space application units were later combined to form the Space Applications Centre (SAC) in 1972.

Sarabhai died on 30 December 1971. SAC was formally created in 1972 from earlier units associated with his work. Therefore, the establishment year of SAC should not be presented as an event personally carried out by Sarabhai in 1972.

Awards and recognition

Sarabhai received the Shanti Swarup Bhatnagar Prize for Physics in 1962 and the Padma Bhushan in 1966. He was awarded the Padma Vibhushan posthumously in 1972.

His contribution was particularly important because he connected scientific research with the creation of institutions capable of sustaining large national programmes.

Prelims focus

  • Vikram Sarabhai: born in Ahmedabad in 1919.
  • He is known as the father of the Indian space programme.
  • PRL: formally established in Ahmedabad on 11 November 1947.
  • INCOSPAR: established in 1962.
  • ISRO: established on 15 August 1969.
  • Trap: PRL was founded in 1947, whereas SAC was formed in 1972.

[Sources: Physical Research Laboratory, 'History,' entries for 1947 and subsequent research fields; Physical Research Laboratory, PRL News: The Spectrum, August 2019, birth-centenary issue on Vikram Sarabhai; Space Applications Centre, 'Founder: Dr. Vikram Ambalal Sarabhai,' biography, institutional work and awards; Space Applications Centre, 'Overview, Genesis and History,' sections on the 1966 earth station and SAC's formation in 1972; ISRO, institutional history and foundation date. Online sources consulted 2 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: A research laboratory in Ahmedabad during the early years of independent India.

body:
Scientific career and principal contribution

Avul Pakir Jainulabdeen Abdul Kalam (1931-2015) was an Indian aerospace scientist. He was born on 15 October 1931 in Rameswaram, Tamil Nadu.

Kalam worked in India's space and defence research programmes. He is closely associated with the successful development of India's early indigenous satellite launch vehicle and later with the country's guided missile development programme.

An artificial satellite is an object placed in orbit around a celestial body. A launch vehicle is a rocket designed to carry a payload, such as a satellite, toward its intended orbit. Developing a satellite and developing a launch vehicle are related but different scientific and technological achievements.

SLV-3 and the Rohini satellite

At ISRO, Kalam served as project director of the Satellite Launch Vehicle-3 (SLV-3) programme. The vehicle was part of India's effort to develop its own satellite-launch capability.

On 18 July 1980, the SLV-3E2 mission successfully placed the Rohini satellite RS-1 into orbit. This was a major achievement because an Indian launch vehicle successfully placed a satellite in orbit.

Aryabhata and Rohini must not be confused

India's first satellite was Aryabhata, launched on 19 April 1975. The satellite was designed and built in India, but it was launched using a Soviet rocket.

The Rohini RS-1 mission of 1980 was different: it demonstrated the ability of an Indian-developed launch vehicle, SLV-3, to place a satellite in orbit.

An earlier SLV-3 experimental mission on 10 August 1979 had been unsuccessful. The success of July 1980 followed this earlier attempt.

Defence research and awards

Kalam later played a leading role in the Integrated Guided Missile Development Programme (IGMDP), launched in 1983. The programme included named missile projects such as Agni and Prithvi. His association with these programmes contributed to his popular identification as the Missile Man of India.

Kalam received the Padma Bhushan in 1981, the Padma Vibhushan in 1990 and the Bharat Ratna in 1997. These are Indian civilian honours, not Nobel Prizes.

He later served as the 11th President of India from 2002 to 2007. His scientific contributions and awards are historical facts independent of changing office-holders.

Prelims focus

  • A. P. J. Abdul Kalam: aerospace science, SLV-3 and IGMDP.
  • Aryabhata: India's first satellite, launched on 19 April 1975 using a Soviet rocket.
  • Rohini RS-1: placed in orbit by SLV-3 on 18 July 1980.
  • IGMDP: launched in 1983.
  • Kalam received the Bharat Ratna in 1997.
  • Trap: India's first satellite and the first successful Indian satellite-launch vehicle represent different achievements.

[Sources: President of India, 'Dr. A. P. J. Abdul Kalam: Profile,' sections on SLV-3, defence research and civilian awards; ISRO, 'Aryabhata,' mission description and launch date; ISRO, 'Experimental Satellites,' entries for Aryabhata, Rohini Technology Payload and Rohini RS-1; ISRO, 'List of SLV Launches,' entries for 1979 and 1980; Defence Research and Development Organisation, historical account of the Integrated Guided Missile Development Programme. Online sources consulted 2 November 2026.]
